pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey in the Kempen of Brabant, founded 1130, keeper of a full-size copy of the Last Supper)
etymology: From Dutch tongeren, a place name, and lo, a clearing in a wood.
biblical_def: Tongerlo in the Antwerp Kempen was founded about 1130 and has been Premonstratensian ever since, with an interruption only between the French suppression of 1796 and the community's return in 1840. It is one of the largest abbeys in Belgium. Its most visited possession is a full-size sixteenth-century copy of Leonardo's Last Supper, painted while the original in Milan was still fresh and now the best evidence of what Leonardo actually painted, since the original has decayed almost past reading. This dictionary records Tongerlo for the irony of a copy preserving an original, and for the supper itself, which is handed down in words rather than paint. Paul says he received the account and passes it on, “For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you” (1Co 11:23). The bread is given with a command, “This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19). The cup is likewise, “Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you” (1Co 11:24), and the meal is a proclamation with an end date, “ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a copy as a transcript from an original; the Lord's Supper as the sacrament of the eucharist; remembrance as the retaining of an idea in the mind; to deliver as to hand over; and a memorial as that which preserves remembrance.
webster_full: COPY, n. A writing like another writing; a transcript from an original; hence, a book, as a copy of the Bible; an imitation; a likeness.
SUPPER, n. The evening meal; the Lord's supper is the sacrament of the eucharist, instituted by our Saviour the evening before his crucifixion.
REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind the idea of a thing formerly known; recollection; honorable memory.
DELIVER, v.t. To hand over; to give or transfer; to put into another's hand or power; to surrender.
MEMORIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; any thing that serves to keep in memory.
scriptures: For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread:
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
corruption_summary: Brabant Premonstratensian abbey of 1130: its sixteenth-century copy now shows what Leonardo painted better than the ruined original does.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Tongerlo's painting illustrates by accident. What is handed on faithfully can outlast what it was taken from, and Paul describes the supper in exactly those terms, as something received and then delivered, “For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you” (1Co 11:23). The transmission is the point.

The second thing is the supper's own character. It is a remembrance with a command attached, “this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19), and a proclamation made with bread and a cup rather than with speech, “ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26). The clause that ends it keeps the table from becoming a museum: the meal is temporary and looks to an arrival. A painting of a supper is a copy of a copy; the supper itself is still being eaten.

pos: n. (the Brabant Premonstratensian abbey of 1128, whose motto is taken from the burning bush)
etymology: From Dutch grim, a personal name or a mask, and bergen, hills.
biblical_def: Grimbergen north of Brussels was founded in 1128 and became Premonstratensian within a few years. It was burnt down three times, in 1142, in 1578 during the religious wars, and again in 1797 after the French suppression, and each time the community rebuilt; its baroque church of 1660 is one of the finest in Belgium. The abbey took for its arms a phoenix in flames with the motto Ardet nec consumitur, it burns and is not consumed, which is a Latin quotation of Exodus. This dictionary records Grimbergen for that motto, because the bush is one of the most loaded images in Scripture. Moses turns aside to a fire that does not destroy what it burns, “the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exo 3:2). God promises the same of his people in flood and flame, “when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned” (Isa 43:2). Three men came out of a furnace untouched, “upon whose bodies the fire had no power” (Dan 3:27), and the fire that does come is for refining rather than for ruin, “though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour” (1Pe 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bush as a shrub with branches; to consume as to destroy by burning; a furnace as an enclosed fireplace for intense heat; to refine as to purify from dross; and a trial as a test or examination.
webster_full: BUSH, n. A shrub with branches; a thick shrub; also, a cluster of shrubs; an assemblage of thick shrubs.
CONSUME, v.t. To destroy by separating the parts of a thing, by decomposition, as by fire, or eating; to destroy utterly.
FURNACE, n. A place where a vehement fire may be made, as for melting ores or metals, or for heating a building.
REFINE, v.t. To purify; to clear from dross, dregs or recrement; as, to refine gold or silver; to purify from what is coarse.
TRIAL, n. Any effort or exertion of strength for the purpose of ascertaining its effect; a test; examination by a test.
scriptures: Exo 3:2
And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
Isa 43:2

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
Dan 3:27

And the princes, governors, and captains, and the king's counsellors, being gathered together, saw these men, upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them.
That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Brabant Premonstratensian abbey of 1128: burnt three times and rebuilt three times, under a motto taken from the bush that was not consumed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the bush actually showed Moses. The remarkable thing was not the fire but the survival of what it burned, which is why the text says both halves, “the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exo 3:2). God afterwards applies the figure to his people under judgment and exile, and is careful not to promise the absence of fire, “when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned” (Isa 43:2).

The second thing is the distinction between fire that destroys and fire that refines. The three in Nebuchadnezzar's furnace were examined afterwards by a crowd looking for damage and found none, “nor was an hair of their head singed” (Dan 3:27). Peter uses the same figure for ordinary trials, and the point is the metal rather than the heat, “That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth” (1Pe 1:7). An abbey burnt three times chose its motto well.

pos: n. (the Flemish Premonstratensian abbey of 1137, whose church the townspeople bought to save it)
etymology: From Latin novum, new, with a Germanic prefix; the new place on the Dender.
biblical_def: Ninove on the Dender in East Flanders was founded in 1137 and given to the Premonstratensians. Its abbey was suppressed by the French in 1796 and the buildings sold for demolition; the great baroque church of 1640 was being broken up for its materials when the inhabitants of Ninove raised money, bought it back in 1822, and made it their parish church, which it remains. This dictionary records Ninove for that purchase, because buying back what is about to be lost is one of Scripture's central transactions and it has a technical name. The law provided for a kinsman to redeem a brother's land, “then shall he redeem that which his brother sold” (Lev 25:25). Boaz does it publicly before witnesses, “Ye are witnesses this day, that I have bought all that was Elimelech's” (Rut 4:9). Jeremiah buys a field in a city about to fall, as a sign, “And I bought the field of Hanameel my uncle's son, that was in Anathoth” (Jer 32:9), and the word is applied to the costliest purchase of all, “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (Eph 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to redeem as to purchase back; a kinsman as a man of the same race or family; a purchase as the acquisition of property by payment; a witness as one who attests a fact; and ransom as the price paid for release.
webster_full: REDEEM, v.t. To purchase back; to ransom; to liberate or rescue from captivity or bondage, or from any obligation or liability to suffer or to be forfeited.
KINSMAN, n. A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.
PURCHASE, n. The acquisition of title or property by one's own act or agreement; the thing purchased.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; a person who knows or sees any thing; one who gives testimony.
RANSOM, n. The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for goods captured by an enemy.
scriptures: If thy brother be waxen poor, and hath sold away some of his possession, and if any of his kin come to redeem it, then shall he redeem that which his brother sold.
Rut 4:9
And Boaz said unto the elders, and unto all the people, Ye are witnesses this day, that I have bought all that was Elimelech's, and all that was Chilion's and Mahlon's, of the hand of Naomi.
Jer 32:9
And I bought the field of Hanameel my uncle's son, that was in Anathoth, and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver.
Eph 1:7
In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace;
corruption_summary: Flemish Premonstratensian abbey of 1137: its church was being demolished for materials when the townspeople bought it back in 1822.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that redemption in Scripture is a commercial word before it is a religious one. The law names a procedure: when a man has lost his land, his nearest kinsman has both the right and the duty to buy it back, “then shall he redeem that which his brother sold” (Lev 25:25), and Boaz executes it in front of the town elders as an ordinary legal act, “Ye are witnesses this day” (Rut 4:9).

The second thing is that such purchases are often made against the odds, as a sign. Jeremiah buys a field in a country the Babylonians are overrunning, and the deed is sealed and stored precisely because the transaction makes no sense yet, “and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver” (Jer 32:9). Paul takes the whole vocabulary and names the price in a clause, “In whom we have redemption through his blood” (Eph 1:7). The people of Ninove bought a roof; the word means more than that, and not less.

pos: n. (the Nottinghamshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1153, head of the English circary, later a ducal palace)
etymology: Old English wella, a spring, and bec, a stream; the spring brook.
biblical_def: Welbeck in Nottinghamshire was founded in 1153 and became the head house of the Premonstratensian circary of England, its abbot visiting every other white-canon house in the country. It was surrendered in 1538 and granted away, and over the following centuries it became one of the great English country houses, seat of the dukes of Portland. The fifth duke, in the nineteenth century, spent a fortune excavating a system of tunnels, an underground ballroom and a subterranean library beneath the park, and lived almost entirely out of sight. This dictionary records Welbeck for the contrast between a house of canons and a buried palace, because Scripture addresses exactly this use of wealth. Haggai rebukes a people living in finished houses while God's house lies waste, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). A man who builds to hide himself is answered, “Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high” (Hab 2:9). A barn-building plan is interrupted, “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee” (Luk 12:20), and what we give was never ours, “all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee” (1Ch 29:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mansion as a dwelling house of considerable size; to excavate as to hollow out; wealth as large possessions; seclusion as separation from society; and ostentation as outward show to excite admiration.
webster_full: MANSION, n. Any place of residence; a house; a habitation; particularly, the house of the lord of a manor.
EXCAVATE, v.t. To hollow; to cut, scoop, dig or wear out the inner part of any thing and make it hollow.
WEALTH, n. Riches; large possessions of money, goods or land; that abundance of worldly estate which exceeds the estate of the greater part of the community.
SECLUSION, n. The act of separating from society or connection; the state of being separate or apart; retirement; privacy.
OSTENTATION, n. Outward show or appearance; ambitious display; vain show, to excite admiration or to draw attention.
scriptures: Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
Hab 2:9
Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil!
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee.
corruption_summary: Nottinghamshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1153, head of the English circary: surrendered in 1538 and turned into a ducal house with a tunnelled underworld.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Haggai's question, which was put to ordinary people rather than to a duke and which concerned priorities rather than architecture, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). Habakkuk adds the motive that Welbeck's tunnels make unusually literal: building in order to be out of reach, “that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil” (Hab 2:9).

The second thing is the interruption. The parable gives a man an excellent plan, adequate resources and no time, and the verdict is one word, “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee” (Luk 12:20). Against all of it stands David's prayer at the gathering of materials for the temple, which is the right posture of a rich man and is almost never the natural one, “for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee” (1Ch 29:14).

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey in the Kempen heath, founded 1140, with its old herb garden and dispensary)
etymology: From Dutch post, a post or boundary marker, and the diminutive ending.
biblical_def: Postel lies in the heathland of the Antwerp Kempen near the Dutch border, founded about 1140 as a grange of Floreffe and raised to an abbey in 1621. The canons are still there. The house has kept a herb garden and a dispensary since the Middle Ages, when the abbey was the nearest thing to a hospital for a wide and empty district, and it still sells the herbs and the cheese. This dictionary records Postel for the dispensary, because Scripture treats medicine and healing without any of the suspicion later piety attached to them. The prophet asks after a known remedy and a known practitioner, “Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?” (Jer 8:22). The Samaritan uses what he has on the wounds, “bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine” (Luk 10:34). God is named the healer of a different wound, “He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psa 147:3), and the last page of Scripture has leaves that are for healing, “the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations” (Rev 22:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines balm as an aromatic plant or ointment; a physician as one skilled in the art of healing; to heal as to cure or restore to soundness; medicine as a substance used to cure disease; and an infirmary as a lodging for the sick.
webster_full: BALM, n. The sap or juice of trees or shrubs remarkably odoriferous or aromatic; any fragrant or valuable ointment; that which heals or soothes distress.
PHYSICIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies for diseases.
HEAL, v.t. To cure of a disease or wound and restore to soundness; to cause to grow sound; to reconcile, as a breach.
MEDICINE, n. Any substance, liquid or solid, that has the property of curing or mitigating disease in animal bodies.
INFIRMARY, n. A lodging or hospital for the sick; an apartment in a monastery or college appropriated to the sick.
scriptures: Jer 8:22
Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?
And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
Rev 22:2

In the midst of the street of it, and on either side of the river, was there the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
corruption_summary: Kempen Premonstratensian house of 1140: its herb garden and dispensary served a district with no doctor, and both are still there.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture nowhere treats remedies as a rival to faith. Jeremiah's famous question assumes both a medicine and a doctor are available and asks why the patient is not better, “Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?” (Jer 8:22). The Samaritan in the parable is commended for competent first aid with ordinary supplies, “pouring in oil and wine” (Luk 10:34).

The live corruption runs both ways: a piety that refuses medicine as faithlessness, and a medicine that imagines it reaches everything. The psalm names a wound that no dispensary stocks a remedy for, and names the physician, “He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psa 147:3). And the last vision of Scripture puts healing in a tree rather than a hospital, extended to whole nations rather than individuals, “the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations” (Rev 22:2). A monastery that grew herbs and prayed was not confused.

pos: n. (the Brabant Premonstratensian abbey of 1134, which runs one of the largest religious publishing houses in the Low Countries)
etymology: From Dutch haver, oats, and bode, a dwelling; or a personal name with bode.
biblical_def: Averbode on the border of Brabant and Limburg was founded in 1134 by Count Arnold II of Loon and given to the Premonstratensians, and the canons are there still. Its baroque church of 1672 by Jan van den Eynde has an unusual oval nave. Since the nineteenth century the abbey's principal public work has been publishing: Averbode produces school magazines and children's periodicals read across Flanders, in editions running to hundreds of thousands. This dictionary records Averbode for that business, because the broadcasting of words is a thing Scripture speaks about in terms of effect rather than effort. God's word is said to accomplish what it was sent for, “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). The commission is as wide as it can be stated, “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). The charge to the preacher allows no convenient season, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2), and the chain of necessity runs backward to a sender, “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to publish as to make known to mankind; the press as the printing press or the business of printing; a periodical as a work published at regular intervals; to disseminate as to scatter as seed; and circulation as the extent to which a thing is spread.
webster_full: PUBLISH, v.t. To discover to mankind; to make known to people in general what before was private or unknown; to divulge; to send a book into the world.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed; particularly, a printing press; hence, the art or business of printing and publishing.
PERIODICAL, n. A paper, magazine or other work published at regular intervals of time.
DISSEMINATE, v.t. To scatter as seed; to sow; to spread; to diffuse; as, to disseminate principles or opinions.
CIRCULATION, n. The act of moving round, or in a circle; a going and returning; also, the extent to which any thing is spread abroad.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
corruption_summary: Brabant Premonstratensian abbey of 1134: its presses print school and children's magazines read across Flanders in hundreds of thousands.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the word carries its own effectiveness. Isaiah does not promise the publisher success; he promises the word will do what it was sent to do, which is a different and more comfortable thing, “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). A press run of three hundred thousand is not the measure of anything, and neither is a press run of three.

The second thing is the breadth of the commission and the inconvenience of the charge. The field is stated as widely as language permits, “preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15), and the timing is deliberately stripped of any excuse, “be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). Paul then runs the chain backwards, from a believer to a hearer to a preacher to a sender, so that nobody at any link can say the matter has nothing to do with him, “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14).

usage: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — effectiveness promised to the word, not the publisher.
“be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — the timing stripped of excuses.
“how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — the chain run backwards to a sender.

pos: n. (the Lincolnshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1154, whose abbot was hanged for the rising of 1536)
etymology: Old English, the people of Bar or Baerla; a settlement name in -ingas.
biblical_def: Barlings in Lincolnshire was founded in 1154 and refounded on its final site soon after. In October 1536 the Lincolnshire Rising broke out against the dissolution of the smaller monasteries and the religious changes behind it; Barlings canons joined the rebels, supplying men and horses, and the abbot Matthew Mackerell was taken, tried, and hanged at Tyburn in 1537. A single fragment of the church tower still stands in a field. This dictionary records Barlings because its abbot's end raises the hardest political question Scripture answers, and the answer is not a slogan in either direction. Civil authority is ordained and resisting it is treated gravely, “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1), “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God” (Rom 13:2). Submission is for the Lord's sake, “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13). And yet when a command runs directly against God's, the apostles disobey openly and say why, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rebellion as open resistance to lawful authority; treason as the offense of attempting to overthrow the government; allegiance as the tie which binds a subject to the state; to submit as to yield to authority; and conscience as the internal judgment of right and wrong.
webster_full: REBELLION, n. An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance; open resistance to lawful authority.
TREASON, n. In the United States, treason is confined to the actual levying of war against the state, or adhering to its enemies.
ALLEGIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; the duty of fidelity to a king, government or state.
SUBMIT, v.t. To let down; to yield, resign or surrender to the power, will or authority of another.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Rom 13:2
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.
Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Lincolnshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1154: its canons joined the rising of 1536 and its abbot was hanged at Tyburn.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture holds two things here that are usually separated for convenience. Paul, writing under Nero, grounds civil authority in God's own ordering and calls resistance to it resistance to God, “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God” (Rom 13:2), and Peter makes the submission an act of worship rather than of prudence, “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13).

But the same apostles, ordered by a lawful council to stop preaching, refused outright and gave the ground, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The distinction is between a command that is unjust and a command that requires sin, and the second is the only warrant Scripture gives. Abbot Mackerell rode out against a king's commissioners over the fate of his house and his lands, which is a different matter from being ordered to deny Christ; the dictionary records his courage and does not call his cause the apostles'.

Greek antitassomai (G498) — to set oneself in array against; “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power”, Romans 13:2.
Greek diatage (G1296) — an ordinance, an arrangement; “resisteth the ordinance of God”, Romans 13:2.
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to place oneself under; “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man”, 1 Peter 2:13.

usage: “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — written under Nero.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — said to a lawful council.
“Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13) — submission as worship, not prudence.

pos: n. (the Leicestershire Premonstratensian abbey of 1160, where King John's body was embalmed)
etymology: Old English Croc, a personal name, and tun, an enclosure; Croc's farmstead.
biblical_def: Croxton Kerrial in Leicestershire was founded about 1160 and became one of the wealthier Premonstratensian houses in England. Its abbot was physician to King John, and when the king died at Newark in October 1216 the abbot embalmed the body; John's bowels were buried at Croxton and the rest of him carried to Worcester. The abbey was dissolved in 1538 and almost nothing remains above ground. This dictionary records Croxton for that grim errand, because the embalming of a king is a blunt reminder of what Scripture says happens to every body including the powerful. The sentence is passed in Eden and is universal, “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19). The Preacher states it as a separation, “Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” (Ecc 12:7). Man's days are compared to grass, “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15), and against all of it Job expects to stand up again in a body, “I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth” (Job 19:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to embalm as to fill a dead body with spices to preserve it; a corpse as the dead body of a human being; dust as fine dry particles of earth; mortality as subjection to death; and the grave as the place of the dead.
webster_full: EMBALM, v.t. To open a dead body, take out the intestines, and fill their place with odoriferous and desiccative spices and drugs, to prevent its putrefaction.
CORPSE, n. The dead body of a human being.
DUST, n. Fine dry particles of earth or other matter, so attenuated that it may be raised and wafted by the wind; earth; the grave.
MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death or the necessity of dying; death; also, frequency of death.
GRAVE, n. A pit or deep place in the earth; the place or receptacle of the dead; the sepulchre.
scriptures: Gen 3:19
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
Ecc 12:7
Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:
corruption_summary: Leicestershire Premonstratensian abbey of 1160: its abbot was King John's physician and embalmed him at Newark in 1216.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the levelling plainness of the sentence. Embalming is an attempt to delay what Scripture states without exception, and the words are addressed to the first man rather than to a criminal, “for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19). The Preacher separates the two halves of a man and sends each where it came from, “and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” (Ecc 12:7).

The second thing is the hope that is not a denial. The psalm's comparison is not meant as consolation, “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15), and Scripture never softens it. What it adds instead is a person and a day, in words Job spoke without any of the apparatus of later theology, “I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25). An abbey keeping a king's entrails under its floor and a parish reciting Job both had the matter about right.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, returning to the giver; “and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it”, Ecclesiastes 12:7.

Hebrew go'el (H1350) — a redeemer, who lives; “I know that my redeemer liveth”, Job 19:25.

“and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” (Ecc 12:7) — the two halves, each sent home.
“I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25) — hope that does not deny the dust.

pos: n. (the Worcestershire Premonstratensian abbey founded by King John in 1215)
etymology: Old English halas, nooks or corners, with the name of Owen, a Welsh prince who held the manor.
biblical_def: Halesowen in what was Worcestershire was founded in 1215 by King John, who granted the manor for the purpose, and the house was settled by Premonstratensians from Welbeck. John's reign had included a six-year papal interdict and his own excommunication, and his religious foundations belong to the years after he submitted. The abbey was dissolved in 1538 and its ruins stand among the buildings of a farm. This dictionary records Halesowen because a king endowing an abbey after a quarrel with the church invites the question Scripture asks about such gifts. God disclaims any need of them, “For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills” (Psa 50:10), “If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof” (Psa 50:12). He is not served as though he lacked anything, “Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing” (Act 17:25). And the escalation of offerings is answered by naming what he actually asks, “Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil?” (Mic 6:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an endowment as a permanent provision for an institution; a benefactor as one who confers a benefit; to atone as to make satisfaction for an offence; an interdict as a prohibition of divine offices; and absolution as a release from guilt.
webster_full: ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of an institution; the fund so settled; also, that which is given or bestowed.
BENEFACTOR, n. He that confers a benefit, especially one who makes charitable contributions either for public institutions or for private use.
ATONE, v.i. To agree; to stand as an equivalent; to make reparation, amends or satisfaction for an offense or a crime.
INTERDICT, n. In the Romish church, a prohibition of the pope, restraining the clergy from performing divine service.
ABSOLUTION, n. In the civil law, an acquittal of a person accused; in the Romish church, a remission of sins by a priest.
scriptures: For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills.
If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof.
Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things;
Mic 6:7
Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?
corruption_summary: Worcestershire Premonstratensian abbey founded by King John in 1215, after an interdict and an excommunication; its ruins stand on a farm.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not a creditor who can be paid off in livestock or masonry. The fiftieth psalm makes the point with a kind of irony, pointing out that he owns everything anybody could bring, “For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills” (Psa 50:10), and that the premise of such giving is absurd, “If I were hungry, I would not tell thee” (Psa 50:12).

The live corruption is giving as settlement, which is not confined to medieval kings. Paul says in Athens that God is not served as though anything could be added to him, “as though he needed any thing” (Act 17:25), and Micah lets a worshipper bid the price up through rams and rivers of oil before answering with the three plain things God does require, “Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil?” (Mic 6:7). An abbey is a fine gift and a poor payment.

“Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil?” (Mic 6:7) — the bidding, and the answer that follows.

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey on the Kent and Sussex border, suppressed by Wolsey in 1525 and later landscaped as a ruin)
etymology: From a Middle English personal name with Old English ham, a homestead.
biblical_def: Bayham on the border of Kent and Sussex was founded about 1208 by the amalgamation of two smaller houses. In 1525 Cardinal Wolsey suppressed it, with other small monasteries, to fund his new colleges at Oxford and Ipswich; local people briefly reinstated the canons by force before the suppression was enforced. In the eighteenth century the owners of the estate had the ruins landscaped, with Humphry Repton advising, so that the broken church became the ornamental centrepiece of a picturesque park. This dictionary records Bayham for that second fate, because Scripture has a settled vocabulary for a holy place made into a spectacle. Ruin becomes a byword, “Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people” (1Ki 9:7). Passers-by are described doing precisely what tourists do, “All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head” (Lam 2:15). A land becomes an astonishment, “To make their land desolate, and a perpetual hissing” (Jer 18:16), and the cause is named, “because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation” (Luk 19:44).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ruin as the remains of a decayed building; picturesque as expressing that which pleases the eye in a landscape; a byword as a common saying or object of scorn; desolation as a wasted place; and astonishment as amazement or confusion of mind.
webster_full: RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; also, in the plural, the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men.
PICTURESQUE, adj. Expressing that peculiar kind of beauty which is agreeable in a picture; striking the mind with great power or pleasure.
BYWORD, n. A common saying; a proverb; also, an object of scorn or contempt mentioned proverbially.
DESOLATION, n. The act of desolating; destruction of inhabitants; a place deprived of inhabitants or otherwise wasted and ruined.
ASTONISHMENT, n. Amazement; confusion of mind from fear, surprise or admiration, at an extraordinary or unexpected event.
scriptures: Then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have hallowed for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people:
Lam 2:15
All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?
To make their land desolate, and a perpetual hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished, and wag his head.
And shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
corruption_summary: Premonstratensian abbey on the Kent border: suppressed by Wolsey in 1525 to fund his colleges, and later landscaped as the ornament of a park.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture describes ruin as something people come to look at, and treats the looking as part of the judgment rather than as harmless curiosity. Solomon is warned at the dedication of the temple itself, “Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people” (1Ki 9:7), and Lamentations records the gestures of the sightseers with painful exactness, “they hiss and wag their head” (Lam 2:15).

The second thing is the cause, which is never merely political. Jeremiah describes a land made into a perpetual hissing, “To make their land desolate, and a perpetual hissing” (Jer 18:16), and the Lord, looking at Jerusalem and weeping, gives the reason in one clause, “because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation” (Luk 19:44). It is worth adding that Wolsey suppressed Bayham thirteen years before Henry suppressed Wolsey's own colleges' endowments, which is its own kind of sermon.
